title: year 4 · the ranges
hook: this part of the path is still being planned: a scribe who won't let the pen stop, and a poet who asks him to understand every line first

segments.voice: Yesterday, Year 4, year close: a year that kept asking questions, and a hymn that ends on perhaps. Did you ask someone an honest question and let them answer? Today is the last day of year four. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-six.

A poet has a story too long to write down himself, so he asks for a scribe. The one who comes is Ganesha. Tradition tells it this way: Vyasa has the Mahabharata in his mind, and Ganesha agrees to write it, on one condition. Once the pen starts, it must not stop. Vyasa agrees, and adds a condition of his own. Ganesha must understand every line before he writes it. That old story belongs on a day like this one. The last day of year four, standing on a ridge, with more ranges in view, and the next one starting with letters.
screen: `A POET WHO NEEDS A SCRIBE.` → `THE PEN MUST NOT STOP.` → `UNDERSTAND EVERY LINE FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the view, said plainly. The next ranges are drawn on the map. Year five begins with Sanskrit for readers: the script, a few words, enough to look at a verse and recognize it. Then come the Puranas, the dharma texts read critically, the Tantras with careful framing, a service capstone, Hinduism around the world, and the great sayings of the Upanishads. Those are the outline. The lessons themselves are still being written and checked, and none of them is approved yet. That's the honest state of this part of the path. Now back to the scribe. The story is a bargain between two kinds of care. Ganesha's condition is about keeping going: no stopping, no waiting around. Vyasa's condition is about slowing down: nothing written that isn't understood. And tradition adds that whenever Vyasa needed time to think, he'd say a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to pause to work it out. So the bargain holds both. Momentum, and understanding. Neither one wins. Turn it once more. Ganesha, the one honored at beginnings, the remover of obstacles, appears here not clearing a road but bent over a page, listening. In some tellings, when his pen breaks mid-story, he snaps off his own tusk and keeps writing, which is why he's pictured with one broken. Whatever a reader makes of that, it's a picture of how a long work actually gets done: a little at a time, without quitting, and without pretending to understand what you don't. Tomorrow, year five starts small, with the letters themselves. A good place for a scribe to begin.
screen: `THE NEXT RANGES ARE DRAWN.` · `THE LESSONS STILL BEING WRITTEN.` · `KEEP GOING, AND UNDERSTAND FIRST.` · `THE BROKEN TUSK, STILL WRITING.` · then, large: `MOMENTUM AND UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the scribe's two conditions, in one sit. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. With one fingertip, trace a slow line on your palm or on the table, as if writing a single letter, and let it take a whole breath. Then another, on the next breath. Keep going, without hurrying, and notice each stroke as it's made. If the mind runs ahead to next year, bring it back to this one line. If you pray, you can begin by remembering Ganesha, honored in Hindu tradition at beginnings. The bell holds the time.
Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the women and the regions, now walked. And the ranges beyond, drawn on the map, still being written. Today's word.

Your line: year four, the ranges. Today, pick up one long thing you'd set down, and do one small piece of it slowly, understanding each step. Tomorrow, the letters. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-six. Year four, done.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Ganesha is remembered at the start of a new undertaking, a journey, a book, a school year or a ceremony, and some images show him as a scribe with a broken tusk.

notes: Last day of year four; the index hook is 'this part of the path is still being planned'. The script says honestly that year five's ranges are drawn in the outline but its lessons are still being written and checked, and that none is approved. No Keeper approval is implied.
Avoids the year-three close (1061: a dotted trail line and Gita 2.40) by using the Vyasa–Ganesha scribe story.

The dictation story: told as 'tradition tells it'. It appears in Ganguli's Adi Parva section 1 (vulgate) and was relegated from the Critical Edition's constituted text; the trapdoor says so. Confirm wording. The knotted verses Vyasa used to buy time are part of the same telling.
The broken tusk as pen is a popular telling, given as 'in some tellings'; other stories explain the tusk differently.

Year five's parts are listed from the outline (Sanskrit for readers, the Puranas, the dharma texts read critically, the Tantras framed, a service capstone, Hinduism in the world, the great sayings); 'the great sayings of the Upanishads' follows the outline's mahavakyas. 'The summit of the ranges' is not named to keep the list short.
howItsDone and the practice say Ganesha is remembered at beginnings 'in Hindu tradition'; confirm wording.
